title: Chapter 2644 - 68: Heart Skill of Causality
content:
Chapter 2644: Chapter 68: Heart Skill of Causality

None of them expected that the Great Chief would personally intervene and kill that guard.

The faces of the Danque Tribe members were all etched with disbelief.

They were puzzled in their hearts, having never anticipated that things would develop in this way.

But after careful reflection, each of them began to understand a bit more.

The cause of this dispute stemmed from the peculiar young man’s "Shaman" identity at the scene.

This was a contest over the authenticity of the Shaman.

But the true struggle was not over the authenticity of the Shaman.

The true struggle was over the Great Chief’s stance.

Everyone’s gaze lingered on the brothers, Dan Bie and Dan Zhu, appraising them silently.

The few who were more insightful glanced at Mo Hua, with thoughts of admiration:

"Lucky boy..."

Even though this "prophecy" was fulfilled, they certainly wouldn’t truly believe Mo Hua was a "Shaman."

Mo Hua’s "prophecy" was deliberately realized by the Great Chief.

In other words, the Great Chief was sparing his life.

In this sense, he actually benefitted from the favor shown to Young Master Dan Zhu.

The Great Chief favored Young Master Dan Zhu and didn’t want his two sons to quarrel again, so he personally intervened, using the guard’s life to settle this dispute and "verify" Mo Hua’s prophecy.

Those with keen eyes could see that Mo Hua’s role was entirely accidental.

It was the Great Chief showing him respect.

As for the so-called Divine Lord’s "revelation," it was simply Mo Hua boasting.

Moreover, how could such a young, clean-shaven pretty boy possibly be a Shaman?

How could he possibly be a servant of the deity?

But regardless, his identity has now been sanctioned by the Great Chief.

Even if no one present truly believed Mo Hua was a Shaman.

As long as he receives the Great Chief’s decree, at least within the Danque Tribe, Mo Hua would officially be considered a genuine Shaman, enjoying special treatment, and no one would dare deny it.

The bet thus concluded.

The banquet also came to an end.

Several servants approached and dragged the dead guard’s corpse away.

The guard’s face was frozen in terror, seemingly unaware of how he died, though perhaps he understood inside that this day would inevitably come.

He just didn’t expect it would arrive so soon.

On the high platform, the beautiful concubine’s face was as pale as paper, desperately suppressing the tremors in her shoulder, not even daring to lift her head to glance at the dead guard.

Others assumed she was frightened by the sight of blood, causing her to lose her composure.

But she understood better than anyone what was truly happening.

Her terror-stricken appearance was fully seen by the Great Chief.

The Great Chief’s expression remained impassive, but there seemed to be a sense of satisfaction in his heart.

Mo Hua’s gaze was calm and composed, yet slightly profound as he observed everything.

...

After the banquet, upon returning to the guest room, it was already very late.

Mo Hua sat cross-legged on the soft animal skin bed, recalling the day’s events, feeling a sense of reflection.

This Great Chief of the Danque Tribe appeared robust and muscular, but his strategies were quite profound.

Moreover, his actions were ruthless, killing decisively.

However, his attitude towards the concubine seemed strange to Mo Hua, differing somewhat from what he had previously understood.

He was the Chieftain, and a concubine consorting with a guard should logically mean killing both of them together, shouldn’t it?

Why punish one to deter another?

Are the concepts here in the Great Wilderness different?

Furthermore, Mo Hua was unclear about how much acknowledgement lay in the Great Chief admitting him as a "Shaman."

Did he truly recognize Mo Hua’s ability as a "Shaman?"

Or was it merely... going with the flow?

Was it that he intended to kill the guard, and Mo Hua predicted it?

Or did Mo Hua’s prophecy ignite the urge to kill within him?

The intertwining of human nature and causality, with its "Ouroboros-like" logic, gave Mo Hua a nuanced insight into "causality."

Is causality objective or a reflection of human nature?

If it’s objective, logically, the Great Chief would have killed that guard regardless.

If it’s influenced by human nature, does it mean that if Mo Hua hadn’t voiced this "prophecy," which sparked the Great Chief’s intention to kill, the guard wouldn’t have died?

Mo Hua pondered deeply, his heart stirred.

The Heavenly Mechanism Causality might merely be a kind of omen, a "revelation," but not an "answer," nor a rigid law.

While studying Heavenly Mechanism Causality, one must not ignore human nature.

In fact, causality itself encompasses the multitudinous changes within human nature.

Human nature is elusive, so causality becomes ever-changing.

And this Danque Tribe, many people here have fairly profound minds.

The Great Chief being able to become the Great Chief is not merely because of being "lustful" or "robust."

Dan Zhu’s third brother, Dan Bie, is indeed not simple.

At least during the banquet, he decisively seized the opportunity to use the accusation of "usurping the Shaman" to try and eliminate Mo Hua.

Although the scheme wasn’t particularly ingenious, Mo Hua had only arrived recently, meeting Dan Bie for the first time.

Within the span of a few bites, Dan Bie already began targeting Mo Hua with a plan.

Moreover, the excuse he used was indeed impeccable.

Like calling Mo Hua a "fraud," a "fake Shaman," deceiving Dan Zhu...

To scheme, to decide, daring to think and act, his timing was precise, his words well-founded.

Even though his goal wasn’t accomplished in the end, evaluating the situation objectively, Dan Bie is undeniably a "talent."

Furthermore, Dan Bie’s attitude towards his younger brother, Dan Zhu, is quite intriguing.
